Context. Both d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 are placed in SCOPe family b.1.2.1 (Fibronectin type III), superfamily b.1.2 (Fibronectin type III), fold b.1 (Immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich), class b (all-beta). Family-level placement is the strongest evolutionary statement SCOPe makes here: it asserts clear sequence/structure evidence of common ancestry between the two domains. The superfamily asserts probable common ancestry across all FN3 domains, and the fold level (shared with Ig domains in b.1.1 and other b.1 superfamilies) asserts only a common seven-strand (A,B,C,C',E,F,G) two-sheet sandwich topology, not homology. A canonical FN3 domain is roughly 90-100 residues. The 'fragment' tag on d1o5dt2 (second domain of chain T in PDB 1O5D, a multi-chain complex entry) means the deposited coordinates for that domain do not cover the complete FN3 fold, either because of construct boundaries or because part of the domain is disordered/unmodelled; it is a statement about coverage of the coordinate set, not about the protein's true domain architecture. I cannot verify the exact missing residues without network access, so the exact extent of the truncation should be read from the SCOPe domain description and residue ranges in the release being used (the annotation is carried in the domain description in SCOPe 2.07/2.08 and is release-specific).

Alignment. (1) Treat the regions absent from d1o5dt2 as missing data, not as deletions or indels relative to d1uc6a1 or other family members. (2) Use local or coverage-aware structural alignment anchored on the strands actually present; do not run global alignment that penalizes end gaps, and do not infer loop-length variation (e.g., in the BC, C'E or FG loops that carry function in FN3 domains) from the fragment. (3) Similarity scores must be normalized by the length of the complete domain (d1uc6a1), not by the fragment length; RMSD or TM-score normalized by the shorter fragment will inflate apparent similarity, while coverage-based scores will understate it. (4) Sequence-identity calculations against the fragment should likewise be reported with coverage, because a short fragment can show misleadingly high or low identity to full-length relatives. (5) Do not use the fragment as a structural template for homology modeling of a complete FN3 domain or for defining family-wide structural core positions; use the complete d1uc6a1 or another full-length family member.

Representative selection. (1) When choosing one representative for the family, superfamily or a sequence-identity cluster, prefer the complete domain d1uc6a1 (or another complete, high-quality domain) over d1o5dt2, even if the fragment has an equal or better resolution/quality score, because ASTRAL SPACI/AEROSPACI-style quality metrics measure crystallographic quality and do not capture completeness. (2) In ASTRAL-style non-redundant subsets at a given identity threshold, a fragment should be deprioritized or filtered; if it survives clustering it may form an artificial singleton cluster simply because it is too short to reach the identity/coverage threshold with its true relatives, which falsely inflates apparent family diversity. (3) Fragment-aware filtering (minimum fraction of the canonical domain length present) should be applied before building benchmark, training or template sets. (4) The fragment remains a valid, classified member of b.1.2.1 and can be retained for completeness of the family listing, but it should be flagged so downstream users do not treat it as a full structural exemplar.

Interpretation of family diversity. (1) The fragment must not be counted as evidence of a shortened or topologically variant FN3 domain; any apparent sequence-length or structural divergence attributable to truncation is an artifact, not real variation within b.1.2.1. (2) Diversity statistics for the family (strand-length distributions, loop variability, core-position conservation, pairwise identity distributions) should be computed from complete domains, or with the fragment weighted/excluded, otherwise variance is overestimated. (3) Function should not be transferred from d1uc6a1 to d1o5dt2 or vice versa on the basis of family membership alone: b.1.2.1 is a large and functionally heterogeneous family (fibronectin repeats, cytokine and hormone receptor extracellular domains, tenascin, titin, neural cell-adhesion molecules, etc.), and FN3 domains that share the fold use different loops and faces for ligand binding (e.g., the RGD loop of fibronectin III10 vs. receptor-ligand interfaces). Family membership supports homology, not a shared binding partner or shared binding site. (4) Any functional or binding-site inference that would lie in the missing region of d1o5dt2 cannot be made from that domain; it would require the complete structure, other chains of the complex, or external experimental evidence. (5) When comparing across SCOPe releases, check whether the fragment annotation, residue boundaries or classification changed, since re-deposition or re-annotation can alter which domains are flagged.

Summary: the fragment tag on d1o5dt2 means it is a legitimate but incomplete b.1.2.1 member. Use coverage-aware local alignment anchored on the complete domain d1uc6a1, choose complete domains as representatives and templates, exclude or down-weight the fragment when quantifying family diversity, and do not transfer specific function between the two domains on the basis of shared family alone.
